newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian official questions N.Z. economic policy.
newsitem.headline: Australian official questions N.Z. economic policy.

text.p: Australian Treasury Secretary Ted Evans, the government's senior economic policy advisor, on Thursday questioned the New Zealand's single-mined focus on low inflation, saying it may be a factor in New Zealand's current account problems.

Evans told an Australian Business Economists luncheon New Zealand was an example where policy-makers focused on inflation and a strong exchange rate to the cost of economic growth and a sustainable current account deficit.
"It is clear it ought to be an issue in the minds of policy makers, that in pursuing one objective one does not undo the other objective," he said.

"It's a question that I would ask for example and have for almost two years of New Zealand -- has the single-minded pursuit of a quite low inflation objective there, which has clearly pushed up their exchange rate, what has that done for their own adjustment process and is that part of the reason that the current account problems have started to emerge."
"The same issue arose in a much clearer case in the form of Mexico," Evans said.
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is independent and has a mandate to target underlying inflation in a zero to three percent band.
It has run a tight monetary policy, with 90 day bill rates currently at 7.32 percent, which has kept the New Zealand dollar firm.

New Zealand's current account deficit has risen to 4.2 percent of GDP in calendar 1996 from 3.7 percent in 1995, its highest level since the 5.1 percent rate reached in 1987. Economists expect the ratio to rise further.
New Zealand exporters have said a high currency has hurt export receipts, while imports have surged as they have become cheaper.

Australian cash rates are set at 6.00 percent and 90 day bills are about the same level. Australia's current account deficit is forecast by the government to fall to 3.75 percent in 1996/97 (July/June) from 4 percent in 1995/96.
